title: Case number 18422
raw:
The facial lesion is soft, compressible, enlarges in the dependent position, and shows low-flow venous channels on imaging—features consistent with a venous malformation rather than an infantile hemangioma.  
CT of the skull base demonstrates absence of the bony carotid canal, confirming congenital internal carotid artery (ICA) agenesis rather than occlusion or dissection.  
CTA images show the agenesis on one side, while the venous malformation is located in the contralateral cheek.

Therefore, the best diagnosis is ICA agenesis with contralateral facial venous malformation.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18428
raw:
The imaging shows a markedly dilated, elongated tubular adnexal structure with thickened enhancing walls and internal fluid, compatible with a hydrosalpinx. The ovary (labeled “O”) is seen separately and appears normal, excluding ovarian torsion or a tubo‑ovarian abscess. The tubular structure demonstrates a twisted configuration and surrounding inflammatory changes on CT and MRI, consistent with torsion of the fallopian tube itself.

There is no imaging evidence of an inflamed appendix, ruptured ovarian cyst, or complex abscess formation. The patient’s age and lack of sexual activity also make PID with tubo‑ovarian abscess unlikely.

The affected side, as shown on the coronal and axial CT/MR (arrowed structure on the patient’s left side), indicates isolated torsion of the left fallopian tube.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18432
raw:
CT images show a solid, lobulated mass adjacent to the liver, isoattenuating to hepatic parenchyma, with subtle surrounding inflammatory change and appearance of a narrow pedicle (yellow arrows). This lesion is separate from the main liver, not cystic (argues against lymphangioma), not hemorrhagic-density (argues against hematoma), and not fluid-like or centered on the pancreas (argues against peripancreatic collection).  

The intraoperative images demonstrate a pedunculated hepatic-appearing lobe with congested, dusky surface consistent with torsion and infarction of an accessory hepatic lobe. This explains the acute epigastric pain in an otherwise healthy young woman.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18433
raw:
CT shows a central mesenteric mass-like area composed of increased-attenuation fat with embedded small soft-tissue nodules and a somewhat spiculated, radiating configuration around mesenteric vessels and small bowel loops, rather than a single solid tumor. There is no large homogeneous nodal mass (as in lymphoma), no discrete aggressive soft-tissue sarcoma, and no single sharply marginated solid desmoid-type mass.  

This mixed fatty/soft-tissue mesenteric lesion with chronic abdominal pain in an older man is characteristic of sclerosing mesenteritis (mesenteric panniculitis), which classically presents as a pseudo-mass of inflamed and fibrotic mesenteric fat.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18443
raw:
MRI shows multiple, bilateral, poorly marginated T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions involving:

- Subcortical and deep white matter in both cerebral hemispheres  
- Deep gray nuclei (thalami, basal ganglia)  
- Brainstem (pons)  

Lesions are relatively symmetric and extensive, without a classic periventricular Dawson’s finger pattern or isolated optic nerve/spinal cord involvement. In a 6‑year‑old with acute onset encephalopathy and seizures 10–11 days after a febrile illness, this pattern is typical of a monophasic post‑infectious demyelinating process.

Multiple sclerosis is unlikely (age, encephalopathy, lesion pattern). NMOSD and MOGAD usually present with optic neuritis and/or myelitis; HIV/PML is inconsistent with the acute presentation and clinical setting.

These clinico‑radiological features best fit acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18445
raw:
The CT of the chest shows extensive anterior chest wall subcutaneous emphysema. Subsequent pelvic and scrotal imaging (radiograph, CT, and ultrasound) demonstrate air outlining the scrotum and within the scrotal sac, with gas tracking along the anterior abdominal wall fascial planes (Camper’s, Scarpa’s, dartos) into the scrotum. There is no evidence of fluid collection, blood, bowel loops, or inflammatory changes of the testes/epididymis.

This combination of chest wall emphysema and gas dissecting into the scrotum after trauma is characteristic of pneumoscrotum.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18459
raw:
The imaging shows multiple, bilateral, poorly marginated lesions involving the deep gray nuclei (thalamus) and cerebellar hemispheres. On MRI they are T2/FLAIR hyperintense with ring‑like or patchy enhancement, but there is no classic MS‑type periventricular “Dawson fingers,” no corpus callosum predilection (as in Susac), no punctate pontine pattern (as in CLIPPERS), and no symmetric hemorrhagic necrosis of bilateral thalami as seen in ANEC.  

Clinically, a 5‑year‑old child developing neurologic symptoms (visual loss, headache, dizziness) about three weeks after a viral infection (hepatitis A) is typical for a post‑infectious demyelinating process. Age, monophasic course, multifocal lesions involving both white matter and deep gray structures, and normal spinal cord strongly support acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18462
raw:
The images show enhancing, tubular structures with flow voids (on MRI) and contrast opacification (on CT) in the retropharyngeal/parapharyngeal space, indicated by arrows. These correspond to the internal carotid arteries, which appear unusually medial and close to the pharyngeal wall. There is no rim‑enhancing fluid collection, gas, or soft-tissue mass to suggest abscess; no hyperdense collection or layering to suggest haematoma; and no amorphous calcification in the prevertebral space typical of longus colli calcific tendinitis. Instead, the imaging demonstrates an anatomic/positional variant of the carotid arteries rather than an inflammatory or hemorrhagic retropharyngeal process.

Thus, the most likely diagnosis is:

Answer: A

title: Case number 18466
raw:
The imaging shows a large right-sided retroperitoneal mass in the region of the right adrenal gland (yellow star on the coronal CT), with heterogeneous enhancement and central necrosis. There is a long, contiguous enhancing tumor thrombus (asterisk) extending from this mass into the inferior vena cava and up into the right atrium, and FDG PET shows high metabolic activity in the mass and thrombus with nodal and pulmonary metastases.

This pattern—adrenal mass with extensive IVC tumor thrombus reaching the right atrium and metastases—is classic for adrenal cortical carcinoma with venous invasion, rather than a primary IVC sarcoma or paraganglioma.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18471
raw:
The CT and PET show a large, irregular, cavitating mass-like consolidation abutting the pleura, with intense FDG uptake and a morphology that mimics a primary lung tumor. Bronchoscopy/EBUS were negative for malignancy, but culture from BAL was positive, indicating an infectious etiology.  

In an immunocompetent patient with a chronic, mass-like pulmonary lesion that crosses segments and closely involves the pleura and chest wall, strongly FDG-avid and mimicking lung cancer, pulmonary actinomycosis is the classic diagnosis. Nocardiosis typically occurs in immunocompromised patients and often shows multiple nodules/abscesses. A simple lung abscess would be more rounded with a clear air–fluid level and would usually be diagnosed clinically without requiring PET and EBUS.  

Thus, the findings best fit pulmonary actinomycosis.  

Answer: A

title: Case number 18472
raw:
The MR scout shows a marked susceptibility artefact in the nasopharyngeal region, suggesting a metallic object.  
Subsequent lateral radiograph and CT images demonstrate a thin, curved, highly radiodense linear structure in the nasopharynx, not attached to bone or teeth and without any history of prior surgery.  
This rules out surgical suture material, calcification, and dental implants, and is most consistent with an accidentally retained metallic object in the nasopharynx.

Therefore, the diagnosis is a **foreign body**.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18473
raw:
MRI demonstrates marked fatty atrophy of both supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, indicating chronic suprascapular neuropathy proximal to the branching of the suprascapular nerve. Axial and oblique images show focal narrowing/compression of the nerve as it passes beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament at the suprascapular notch, without evidence of an ossified bony bar, hypertrophic/ossified ligament, paralabral cyst, or scapular bone anomaly.  

The combination of SSp and ISp atrophy with direct imaging of nerve entrapment at the suprascapular notch by a normal (non‑ossified) STSL best fits:

Answer: A

title: Case number 18475
raw:
The images show imperforate anus on MRI, together with malformations of the hands and feet. The hand radiographs demonstrate abnormal thumbs (triphalangeal / dysplastic thumbs with otherwise normal radius and ulna), and there is evidence of associated renal anomaly on abdominal MRI. This combination of imperforate anus, radial–thumb malformations without radial aplasia, and other anomalies is characteristic of Townes–Brocks syndrome, rather than BOR, Okihiro (which typically has radial aplasia), VACTERL association, or Goldenhar syndrome.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18483
raw:
The skull imaging shows a solitary, well‑circumscribed calvarial defect in the right parietal bone, without associated soft-tissue mass, periosteal reaction, or aggressive bone destruction. The borders are smooth, with no intracranial extension and normal underlying brain parenchyma.

Clinically, the defect appeared shortly after minor trauma, with initial local swelling that subsided and left a palpable depression, and the child is otherwise well with normal labs. This evolution and the benign imaging appearance fit a post‑traumatic lytic calvarial lesion (likely due to resorption around an intraosseous hematoma or a post-traumatic “bone cyst”).

Ewing sarcoma and lymphoma/leukemia would typically present with painful, aggressive lesions and systemic abnormalities. A vascular malformation should show characteristic flow voids or enhancing vascular channels, which are absent. A giant parietal foramen is congenital and usually bilateral and parasagittal near the midline, whereas this defect is unilateral, correlating with a recent trauma.

Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is a posttraumatic lytic skull lesion.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18484
raw:
CT images show a whirl sign (twisting of mesentery and vessels) in the right lower abdomen, with markedly dilated colon extending upward and interposed between the liver and right hemidiaphragm (Chilaiditi’s sign), seen on both CT and abdominal radiograph as haustrated gas under the right hemidiaphragm. Clinically there is a palpable painful mass in the right upper quadrant, consistent with a distended, displaced cecum.

These findings indicate a twisted and displaced cecum causing cecal volvulus, with the distended cecum interposed between liver and diaphragm, i.e., cecal volvulus associated with Chilaiditi’s sign.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18486
raw:
The MRI shows an acute brainstem lesion in the pons with high signal on T2/FLAIR and corresponding restricted diffusion on DWI/ADC, consistent with an acute infarct in the pontine region causing the internuclear ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and dysarthria.

The key clinical clue is the combination of:
- Elderly male
- Known myelodysplastic syndrome
- Relapsing polychondritis

This triad is characteristic of VEXAS (Vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X‑linked, Autoinflammatory, Somatic) syndrome, an adult-onset autoinflammatory disease that frequently coexists with myelodysplastic syndromes and chondritis, and can manifest CNS vasculitis with stroke-like events.

Among the options, this pattern most specifically fits VEXAS syndrome rather than nonspecific vasculitis, CLIPPERS, ADEM, or infection.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18489
raw:
The CT images show bilateral kidneys with a diffusely hypoenhancing cortical band and relatively preserved enhancing medulla, giving a circumferential cortical non-enhancement pattern rather than focal wedge-shaped defects. This is symmetric and bilateral, consistent with diffuse cortical ischemia.  

In a 66-year-old patient with severe post-surgical hypoperfusion and multiorgan failure, such a pattern is typical of acute cortical renal necrosis due to global ischemic insult, rather than focal embolic infarcts, infection, or venous thrombosis.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18491
raw:
The ultrasound images show two separate, homogeneous ovoid structures with identical echotexture and echogenicity to normal testicular tissue within the left hemiscrotum. They are adjacent, with one anterior to the other, and there is no cystic component, calcification, or heterogeneous solid mass to suggest tumour, dermoid, or haemorrhagic cyst. There is also no serpiginous, vascular pattern to suggest varicocele.  

This appearance of a firm, non-tender scrotal mass composed of normal-appearing testicular parenchyma is characteristic of a supernumerary testis.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18499
raw:
The lesions are small, round, well-circumscribed structures at the renal hila bilaterally, enhancing identically to the arterial system on CT and MR angiography, and they are clearly continuous with renal arterial branches. There is no solid parenchymal mass or cystic component.

On color Doppler ultrasound, each lesion shows a classic “yin‑yang” pattern (opposed red and blue within the same sac), indicating swirling flow within a focal arterial dilatation. There is no tangle of vessels or early venous filling that would suggest an arteriovenous malformation.

These findings are characteristic of renal artery aneurysms, not adrenal/pheochromocytoma, parapyelic cysts, or clear cell tumors.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18502
raw:
Multiloculated, T2‑hyperintense cystic structures are seen arising from the posterior inferior glenoid (yellow arrows), consistent with a paralabral cyst. The cyst extends laterally/inferiorly into the quadrilateral space (blue arrows). There is denervation change/atrophy in the teres minor muscle (red arrows), which is innervated by the axillary nerve that traverses the quadrilateral space.  

These findings indicate axillary nerve compression by a paralabral cyst in the quadrilateral space – i.e., quadrilateral space syndrome secondary to a paralabral cyst – rather than a simple seroma, hematoma, isolated paralabral cyst, or spinoglenoid varices.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18507
raw:
The images show an angiographic series of the iliac arterial system with a branch supplying a transplanted kidney. There is a focal, tight stenosis at the anastomotic origin of this branch. Subsequent images demonstrate passage of a balloon and then deployment of a stent across this stenotic segment, with restoration of normal caliber and improved perfusion of the transplanted kidney.

This corresponds to treatment of transplant renal artery stenosis, not the main external iliac artery or any venous structure. Therefore, the best diagnosis is a post-transplant renal artery stent.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18510
raw:
The radiographs and CT show a complex distal tibial fracture:

- There is a metaphyseal fracture line in the distal tibia.
- The fracture extends through the physis.
- CT axial images show a sagittal fracture component through the epiphysis, with separation of the anterolateral portion of the tibial plafond.
- Thus, the fracture involves metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis in three planes—a classic “triplane” pattern.
- The main epiphyseal fragment is located laterally, which corresponds to a lateral triplane fracture rather than a medial variant.

This pattern is not a simple Salter–Harris II (metaphysis + physis) or III (epiphysis + physis) injury, and is more complex than a Tillaux (pure SH III anterolateral epiphyseal) fracture.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18511
raw:
Ultrasound shows multiple, well-defined, homogeneous, solid nodules arising from the tunica along the surface of the left testis, indenting but not infiltrating the parenchyma. They are isoechoic–slightly hypoechoic relative to testis and show some internal/peripheral vascularity on Doppler. The lesions are small and multifocal, without a dominant large aggressive mass or diffuse scrotal wall thickening.

In a 24‑year‑old man, this appearance best corresponds to multifocal adenomatoid tumors of the tunica albuginea, a benign mesothelial neoplasm known to present as multiple capsular nodules. Fibrous pseudotumor would typically be more echogenic and avascular, and the malignant options (rhabdomyosarcoma, mesothelioma, leiomyosarcoma) usually present as larger, more infiltrative masses rather than numerous small capsular nodules.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18517
raw:
The MRI shows a heterogeneous, poorly marginated lesion involving the outer posterior myometrium of the uterus, with small cystic/hemorrhagic foci (white arrow) and continuity with a T1‑hyperintense focus on the uterine serosa (last image), compatible with hemorrhagic ectopic endometrial tissue. This pattern corresponds to adenomyosis arising from the serosal surface (external adenomyosis) rather than a classic intramural leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma, or isolated deep infiltrating endometriosis.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18521
raw:
The CT angiography shows a markedly abnormal **left lung**: reduced volume, reticular–septal thickening and fibrosis, and multiple dilated subpleural/pleural vessels, with shift of the mediastinum toward the left on the chest radiograph. The pulmonary arteries are well opacified without intraluminal filling defects, so acute pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection are not supported.

Critically, there is **absence/abrupt termination of the left pulmonary veins entering the left atrium**, with development of collateral systemic veins (seen along the pleura and chest wall and extending into the abdomen). This chronic unilateral venous obstruction explains the prior CT description of mosaic attenuation and fibrosis and the long history of recurrent pulmonary infections.

This pattern is classic for **unilateral pulmonary vein atresia** rather than COPD exacerbation, MI, or PE.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18537
raw:
The imaging shows:

- Axial US with two symmetric neural elements → split cord, consistent with diastematomyelia.  
- CT spine demonstrates a midline bony spur in the thoracic canal, confirming diastematomyelia.  
- MRI reveals a large CSF-intensity posterior sac connected to the spinal canal by a narrow neck. Within the dorsal aspect of the cord at this level is a focal cystic dilatation of the central canal (highlighted by the orange arrow), which is continuous with the neck of the sac—features of a dorsal myelocystocele. A fibroneural stalk tethers the cord to the sac wall (limited dorsal myeloschisis).

These findings indicate a closed spinal dysraphism (no open placode as in myelomeningocele and not a simple CSF sac as in meningocele) with a saccular component containing a myelocystocele and associated diastematomyelia.

This matches:

A. Thoracic saccular limited dorsal myeloschisis (myelocystocele type) with diastematomyelia

Answer: A

title: Case number 18543
raw:
MRI shows symmetric cortical diffusion restriction predominantly involving the bilateral frontal–parietal cortices and cingulate/parasagittal regions (DWI hyperintensity with corresponding low ADC). There is also T1 hyperintensity of the globus pallidus and midbrain, a classic sign of chronic hepatic encephalopathy from manganese deposition in cirrhosis.

In a cirrhotic patient with acute deterioration in sensorium, this combination of acute cortical diffusion restriction in characteristic regions plus chronic pallidal T1 hyperintensity is most consistent with acute hyperammonemic/hepatic encephalopathy.

Carbon monoxide poisoning, hypoglycemic encephalopathy, CJD, and generic hypoxic insult would not account for the characteristic pallidal T1 hyperintensity and typical distribution tied to liver disease.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18545
raw:
The CT images of the left ilium and sacrum show expanded bone with cortical thickening and mixed lytic–sclerotic changes, along with coarsened trabeculae—classic for Paget’s disease. There is no evident aggressive periosteal reaction, cortical destruction with large soft-tissue mass, or other features to suggest sarcomatous transformation or primary osteosarcoma. The patient is asymptomatic, and this is an incidental finding in a typical age group and location (pelvis) for Paget’s disease. Osteomyelitis and metastasis are less likely given the pattern and lack of systemic/inflammatory signs.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18556
raw:
MRI images show a longitudinal, CSF–signal intensity cavity within the central spinal cord extending over several segments, without evidence of compressive spondylotic changes or a discrete mass. The cord is not split into two hemicords, and there is no tumour or marked canal stenosis. This appearance is characteristic of a syrinx.

Given the central intramedullary fluid-filled cavity and the patient’s progressive limb weakness, the most likely diagnosis is:

Answer: C

title: Case number 18564
raw:
The images show:

- Thickened, enhancing tissue around the cavernous sinuses / clivus with dural involvement → hypertrophic pachymeningitis.
- Black-blood post‑contrast MRI and 3D TOF MRA demonstrate bilateral cavernous internal carotid artery wall enhancement and stenosis → intracranial vasculitis.
- DWI/ADC show restricted diffusion in the brainstem region → ischemia/infarcts from vasculitis.
- Head CT shows skull base / temporal bone changes.
- Chest CT reveals multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules.

An 11‑year‑old with severe headaches, diplopia, LOC, weight loss, skull-base pachymeningitis, intracranial vasculitis, and multiple lung nodules is most consistent with a systemic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis involving respiratory tract and CNS—i.e., granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

The other options either do not explain the systemic lung nodules (Tolosa–Hunt, IgG4-related disease), do not typically cause this pattern of vasculitis with lung nodules (neurosarcoidosis), or more commonly show basal exudative meningitis and different chest patterns (tuberculous pachymeningitis).

Answer: A

title: Case number 18575
raw:
The imaging and clinical findings point to a multisystem developmental syndrome:

- Panoramic radiograph and jaw CT show multiple expansile cystic lesions of the mandible/maxilla, consistent with multiple odontogenic keratocysts.
- Head CT and 3D skull reconstruction show calcification along the falx cerebri and craniofacial anomalies.
- Chest radiograph shows rib anomalies (bifid ribs).
- Cervical spine radiograph suggests vertebral anomalies.
- Photograph of the palms reveals multiple small pits.

This combination—multiple odontogenic keratocysts, falx cerebri calcification, bifid ribs, vertebral anomalies, and palmar pits—is characteristic of nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin–Goltz syndrome).

Other options (pseudohypoparathyroidism, seborrheic keratosis, Rombo syndrome, unilateral nevoid BCC with comedones) do not produce this specific constellation of jaw cysts plus skeletal and palmar findings.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18581
raw:
The MRI (DWI/ADC/FLAIR) shows acute infarcts in the left frontoparietal region. CTA and DSA images of the neck and intracranial circulation demonstrate bilateral, multifocal areas of stenosis with intervening dilatations in the extracranial internal carotid arteries, creating a classic “string-of-beads” appearance. This pattern is characteristic of fibromuscular dysplasia, especially in a young woman, and is not typical for isolated atherosclerosis, dissection, moyamoya disease (which would show terminal ICA/proximal MCA/ACA narrowing with basal collaterals), or congenital ICA hypoplasia (diffusely small-caliber vessels).

Therefore the most likely diagnosis is fibromuscular dysplasias.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18582
raw:
The CT shows:

- Chest: Numerous, bilateral, peripheral nodules with central low attenuation/cavitation—typical of septic emboli/pyogenic pulmonary abscesses rather than classic upper-lobe, tree-in-bud or miliary patterns of tuberculosis or solid metastatic nodules.
- Abdomen: Both kidneys contain multiple low-attenuation, rim‑enhancing lesions consistent with renal abscesses.
- Pelvis: An enlarged prostate with a central low-attenuation, rim‑enhancing collection (prostatic abscess), with adjacent pelvic/retroperitoneal collections and possible psoas/paravertebral abscesses.

This constellation is best explained by disseminated pyogenic (bacterial) infection producing multiple abscesses in different organs. The prompt mention of HIV, HBV, HCV, and TB testing reflects evaluation for an underlying immunocompromised state, but the direct radiologic diagnosis is widespread pyogenic infection with multiple organ abscesses, not prostate cancer metastases or classic tuberculosis.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18585
raw:
The lesion is in a 1‑year‑old child and presents as a slowly enlarging indurated plaque in the pubic/inguinal region. Imaging shows a poorly marginated subcutaneous lesion, predominantly plaque-like, with a mixed fibrous and fatty appearance on MRI and heterogeneous echogenicity on ultrasound—features characteristic of a triphasic fibrous/fatty/mesenchymal lesion.  

This combination of age (infancy), typical anatomic location (inguinal–genital region), plaque-like subcutaneous involvement, and mixed fibrofatty imaging appearance is classic for fibrous hamartoma of infancy.  
Desmoid fibromatosis is usually deeper and purely soft-tissue without interspersed fat; dermatomyofibroma and plaque-like myofibroblastic tumour are largely dermal and not prominently fibrofatty; plexiform myofibroblastoma typically occurs in adults.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18596
raw:
MRI shows an ill‑defined intramuscular lesion in the supraclavicular region with:

- Predominant fatty signal (T1 hyperintense areas, star) infiltrating muscle  
- Thick low‑signal fibrous septa and bands (arrows)  
- Scattered small venous channels / phlebolith on US (echogenic focus) with minimal flow  
- Patchy enhancement without features of a high‑flow lesion or aggressive sarcoma

This combination of intramuscular fibrofatty overgrowth with dysplastic low‑flow venous channels is characteristic of a fibro‑adipose vascular anomaly (a specific subtype of venous malformation), rather than a pure venous malformation, intramuscular haemangioma, PTEN hamartoma, or soft‑tissue sarcoma.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18602
raw:
CT shows bilateral, patchy, predominantly peripheral and basal consolidations with ground-glass opacities and some perilobular pattern, sparing much of the upper lobes. There is no discrete mass, no significant lymphadenopathy, and no classic crazy-paving.

This pattern, together with subacute symptoms following a viral infection (SARS‑CoV‑2) and non-resolution despite antibiotics, is characteristic of organizing pneumonia. Post–COVID organizing pneumonia is well recognized and radiologically indistinguishable from cryptogenic organizing pneumonia.

Alveolar sarcoidosis would typically show perilymphatic nodules and known systemic sarcoidosis; invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma or lymphoma would more often present as focal or lobar “pneumonic-type” consolidation or mass with possible lymphadenopathy; alveolar proteinosis classically shows diffuse crazy-paving rather than these patchy consolidations.

Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is organizing pneumonia.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18608
raw:
The fetal MRI shows a midline cystic lesion in the sacral region, projecting posteriorly and filled with CSF signal. The lesion is covered by skin and there is no herniation of neural tissue into the sac, so this represents a closed spinal dysraphism rather than an open myelomeningocele. There are no associated anterior abdominal wall defects, bladder exstrophy, or imperforate anus to suggest OEIS complex, and no presacral/anterior meningocele or hemisacrum to suggest Currarino syndrome. The configuration is of a simple posterior meningocele rather than a dilated terminal central canal characteristic of a terminal myelocystocele.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18624
raw:
The imaging shows a well-defined, elongated mass along the course of the falciform ligament anterior to the left hepatic lobe. On CT it is hyperdense, consistent with acute/subacute blood. On MRI it is markedly hyperintense on T1-weighted fat-suppressed sequences and shows little to no contrast enhancement, again compatible with a blood collection rather than a vascular structure or solid tumor.  

Clinically, the patient is on warfarin (stopped on admission) and has no history of trauma, making a spontaneous intraperitoneal hemorrhage plausible. The location and imaging characteristics specifically support a hematoma confined to the falciform ligament rather than torsion, cyst, mesothelioma, or venous engorgement.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18625
raw:
Radiographs of the hands and feet show a **severe, symmetric, erosive polyarthritis** involving MCPs, PIPs, and especially DIPs and MTPs, with marked marginal erosions and joint destruction rather than the pattern of non‑erosive IBD‑related arthritis or degenerative osteoarthritis.  

Clinically, the patient has inflammatory polyarthritis plus **erythematous papules on the face and chest**, which is classic for **multicentric reticulohistiocytosis**, characterized by papulonodular skin lesions and a rapidly destructive, symmetric arthritis of the small joints (often including DIPs).  

Psoriatic arthritis would require typical psoriatic plaques/nail changes; gout would show asymmetric, punched‑out tophaceous erosions, and IBD‑related arthritis is generally non‑erosive and lacks this skin eruption. Erosive OA does not match the systemic rash and this degree/distribution of erosions.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18629
raw:
The radiographs show a lateral patellar dislocation. On the coronal fat-suppressed MRI images, there is a complete distal tear of the medial collateral ligament from its tibial attachment. The torn MCL is displaced proximally/superficially, with the pes anserine tendons interposed between the ligament and its tibial insertion (blue vs green arrows), which is characteristic of a Stener-like lesion of the MCL. This occurs in the setting of a multiligament injury given the concurrent patellar dislocation.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18636
raw:
The liver imaging (US, CT, MRI) shows focal lesions without classic central necrosis or rim-enhancing abscess characteristics. Chest CT shows bilateral hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy and small pulmonary nodules, suggesting a systemic granulomatous process.  

Histology from the liver lesion demonstrates well-formed granulomas with multinucleated giant cells and no obvious central caseation, which is typical of noncaseating granulomas. This favors sarcoidosis rather than tuberculosis (which usually shows caseating necrosis) or IgG4-related disease (which features storiform fibrosis and IgG4+ plasma cells).  

Taken together—systemic involvement (lung and liver), noncaseating granulomas on histology, and absence of features typical for abscess or metastases—the most likely diagnosis is abdominal sarcoidosis.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18638
raw:
The imaging shows a small, hook-like exostotic projection arising from the medial proximal tibial metaphysis, at the insertion site of the pes anserinus tendons. It is cortically based, without aggressive features or soft-tissue mass, and occurs in a young adolescent with knee pain. This appearance and location are characteristic of a traction-type exostosis at the pes anserine insertion rather than a generic osteochondroma or other parosteal/reactive lesions.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18646
raw:
The CT and perfusion maps show an acute right MCA territory infarct. CTA/DSA demonstrate tapering stenosis and irregularity of the cervical internal carotid artery consistent with a dissection. In addition, the bone-window CT highlights an elongated styloid process projecting toward the ICA. This combination indicates a carotid artery dissection caused by compression from an elongated styloid process (Eagle syndrome), leading to embolic stroke in this young woman.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18670
raw:
Imaging shows massive bilateral cystic replacement of cerebral parenchyma with a very thin cortical mantle and marked ventriculomegaly. This reflects a destructive process leading to cystic encephalomalacia and secondary ex‑vacuo ventricular enlargement, rather than a pure obstructive hydrocephalus (where parenchyma is preserved) or focal porencephalic/subependymal cysts. TORCH infection would classically show calcifications and microcephaly, which are not evident here.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18673
raw:
The lesion is a well-defined, ovoid structure with a dense central calcification and surrounding soft-tissue rim on CT, appearing as a central echogenic focus with acoustic shadowing on ultrasound, and as a discrete calcified mass in the right groin on radiograph. The gross specimen is a smooth, white “boiled egg–like” body, typical of a giant peritoneal loose body.  

Clinically it presented as a non-reducible right inguinal swelling consistent with an inguinal hernia; the images show this loose body located within the hernia sac rather than free in the scrotal cavity. There is no history or imaging evidence suggesting a foreign body, teratoma, or calcified fibrous pseudotumour.  

Answer: A

title: Case number 18674
raw:
CT shows multiple, predominantly peripheral cavitary nodules and consolidations in the right lung, some with surrounding ground-glass change, rather than thin‑walled air spaces (bullae) or upper-lobe–predominant cavities. There is no mention of rheumatoid disease or sarcoidosis, which would be expected if options A or E were correct. Mycobacterial infection typically shows apical cavitation and tree‑in‑bud nodularity, which is not evident here.

In a recent COVID‑19 patient, multiple cavitary nodules with halo-like ground glass strongly suggest angioinvasive fungal infection (e.g., aspergillosis) rather than the other listed causes.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18684
raw:
The imaging shows a large, predominantly homogeneous soft‑tissue mass in the right parapharyngeal space with submucosal expansion of the lateral pharyngeal wall and tonsillar region, but intact mucosa. It involves/occupies both pre‑ and post‑styloid PPS without a clear origin from parotid gland, nasopharyngeal mucosa, or masticator space, so it is best considered a primary PPS lesion rather than invasion from a neighboring space.

The lesion enhances fairly homogeneously, shows marked diffusion restriction on DWI/ADC, and is intensely FDG‑avid on PET. There is associated right supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. This pattern — homogenous infiltrative mass with strong diffusion restriction and FDG uptake, submucosal growth, and nodal disease in a young adult — is characteristic of extranodal lymphoma rather than salivary malignancy, sarcoma, or metastatic deposits.

Therefore the best single diagnosis is:

Answer: C

title: Case number 18697
raw:
The CT images show a large, predominantly right-lobe liver mass with intense arterial hyperenhancement and heterogeneous internal architecture. Subsequent angiographic images demonstrate a marked tumor blush supplied by branches of the hepatic artery, with selective catheterization and embolization—typical of a hypervascular primary liver malignancy targeted for transarterial therapy.  

In this 85-year-old woman, benign entities such as hepatic adenoma and focal nodular hyperplasia are highly unlikely (they occur predominantly in younger women and usually with normal or minimally abnormal liver tests). Metastases more often present as multiple, often hypovascular lesions. Mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma typically shows delayed, progressive enhancement rather than this strong arterial hypervascular pattern.

The imaging and clinical context most strongly support hepatocellular carcinoma.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18703
raw:
The images show a small, extra-axial lesion at the skull base/petrous region. On CT it appears as a very dense, nodular, ring‑like calcified mass. On MRI it is predominantly signal void (markedly hypointense) on T2/T1 with minimal surrounding effect, consistent with a heavily calcified, fibrous lesion rather than a vascular malformation or intra-axial tumor.

This pattern—an extra-axial, intensely calcified mass in the skull base/CP angle region with low signal on all MRI sequences—is classic for a calcifying pseudoneoplasm of the neuraxis (CAPNON), a rare benign lesion that can present with headaches, dizziness, and seizures.

Cavernous malformation, oligodendroglioma, metastatic calcifications, and granulomas typically show different locations and imaging characteristics (less dense calcification, intra-axial, or different enhancement patterns).

Answer: B

title: Case number 18716
raw:
The CT angiography shows a curvilinear filling defect and irregular narrowing in the proximal left renal artery, compatible with an intimal flap and double lumen—i.e., a renal artery dissection. In the same segment there is a focal saccular contrast-filled outpouching rather than a fusiform dilation, and there is adjacent perinephric/renal parenchymal hemorrhage, which is typical of a pseudoaneurysm (contained rupture) rather than a true aneurysm.  

The DSA and 3D reconstructions confirm a dissected segment of the left renal artery giving rise to a saccular pseudoaneurysm, with associated segmental renal infarction.  

This combination best fits a renal artery dissection complicated by pseudoaneurysm formation.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18717
raw:
The CT shows a small, well-circumscribed, homogeneous soft-tissue mass arising from the wall of the distal oesophagus/GE junction, projecting exophytically into the mediastinum. There is no evidence of necrosis, heterogeneity, invasion, or multiple lesions.

Among the options:
- GISTs and leiomyosarcomas are typically larger, more heterogeneous, and often show necrosis or aggressive features.
- Schwannomas and metastatic lesions would less characteristically present as a solitary, smooth, intramural esophageal mass of this appearance.

These imaging features are classic for a benign oesophageal leiomyoma, the most common benign tumour of the oesophagus.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18723
raw:
The mesenteric imaging shows a well-defined soft tissue mass with radiating strands encasing mesenteric vessels, producing a desmoplastic reaction – classic for mesenteric metastasis from a small-bowel carcinoid. The liver shows multiple hypervascular lesions on CT, typical of carcinoid hepatic metastases.  

Given the history of previous ileal mass resection (likely carcinoid) and the absence of a demonstrated new ileal mural mass on these images, this constellation best represents metastatic mesenteric and hepatic disease occurring years after resection of a primary ileal carcinoid, rather than a new/recurrent primary ileal lesion, lymphoma, or sclerosing mesenteritis.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18734
raw:
The MRI shows a large lobulated, predominantly intraventricular mass arising from the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle in a young child, causing obstructive hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. The lesion is well-defined without clear parenchymal invasion, favoring a benign choroid plexus tumor over carcinoma.

Histology demonstrates papillary fronds lined by a single layer of uniform cuboidal epithelium without significant atypia, necrosis, or increased mitotic activity—features characteristic of a classic choroid plexus papilloma (WHO grade I), not atypical papilloma or carcinoma. The appearance is not consistent with meningioma or central neurocytoma.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18735
raw:
The images show a small, well-circumscribed, intensely enhancing nodular lesion in the left parasellar/interpeduncular cistern region, along the expected cisternal course of the oculomotor nerve. It appears intra‑cisternal rather than dural-based (no broad dural attachment or tail, and no skull base hyperostosis), arguing against meningioma or dural metastasis. The lesion is extra-axial and localized along a single cranial nerve, matching the clinical finding of an isolated left oculomotor nerve palsy. This constellation is most consistent with an oculomotor nerve schwannoma.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18743
raw:
Ultrasound shows an ill‑defined, predominantly echogenic mass between the anterior abdominal wall and underlying bowel, with surrounding hypoechoic inflammatory change.  
On CT this corresponds to an ovoid fatty lesion in the right iliac fossa, located between the cecum/ascending colon and the abdominal wall, with heterogeneous attenuation and surrounding fat stranding but no clear inflamed bowel wall or tubular appendiceal remnant.  
MRI demonstrates a mass with central high signal and peripheral enhancement plus restricted diffusion, compatible with necrotic/infected fat rather than solid bowel or adnexal pathology.

There is no imaging evidence of an enlarged torsed ovary, inflamed bowel segment, stump appendix, or cecal diverticulum. The appearance and location are classic for omental infarction that has become secondarily infected.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18749
raw:
The oesophagogram shows a normal, continuous esophageal lumen from pharynx to stomach without atresia. At the mid-cervical level there is a small contrast-filled tract connecting the esophagus to the airway (highlighted by arrows), consistent with an isolated tracheoesophageal fistula.  

Clinically, the child has had symptoms (cough, aspiration pneumonitis, regurgitation) since early infancy, supporting a congenital lesion rather than an acquired fistula. The intact esophagus rules out types A–D (which involve esophageal atresia).  

This pattern corresponds to the “H-type” congenital tracheoesophageal fistula, also known as type E.  

Answer: E

title: Case number 18752
raw:
Multiple imaging modalities show innumerable small, relatively homogeneous hypoechoic liver lesions on ultrasound and corresponding hypoattenuating nodules on CT, with similar lesions in the spleen. On MRI the lesions are T1 hypointense, mildly T2 hyperintense and show diffusion restriction, compatible with solid cellular masses rather than fat (steatosis) or necrotic cavities (abscesses). There is no characteristic arterial hyperenhancement and washout to suggest multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma. Multifocal steatosis would show signal dropout on opposed-phase imaging rather than discrete solid nodules, and metastases are less likely than a lymphoma in the setting of severe untreated HIV, with simultaneous liver and splenic involvement and B symptoms.

The constellation of constitutional symptoms, severe immunosuppression, and the imaging pattern of multiple solid lesions in liver and spleen is most typical of lymphoma.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18758
raw:
The CT images of the left breast and chest wall show extensive soft‑tissue gas with a mottled, bubbly pattern tracking along fascial planes (highlighted by the arrows), rather than a confined fluid collection. This pattern indicates a rapidly progressive, gas-forming infection involving the fascia and subcutaneous tissues, not just a localized abscess. The patient’s risk factors (diabetes, obesity) and rapid clinical deterioration despite antibiotics further support necrotising fasciitis over cellulitis, mastitis, or a simple abscess. Inflammatory breast cancer would not exhibit gas in the tissues.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18762
raw:
The imaging shows a well-defined lytic lesion in the lateral proximal tibia with a relatively thin shell of reactive bone and cortical breach, filled with soft tissue density on MRI and CT. There is little periosteal reaction and the systemic inflammatory markers are low, indicating a chronic “cold” process rather than acute pyogenic infection.  

The postoperative radiograph shows filling of the cavity with beads (antibiotic beads), and the histology slide demonstrates granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and necrosis, compatible with tuberculous osteomyelitis rather than pyogenic osteomyelitis, sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, or metastasis.

This best fits an intraosseous cold abscess of tuberculous origin.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18771
raw:
The CT images show a right-sided retrobulbar hematoma with marked proptosis. The posterior globe is indented with a pointed (“tenting”) configuration and decreased posterior globe angle, indicating increased intraorbital pressure. The optic nerve appears stretched. These are classic imaging findings of raised orbital compartment pressure causing globe tenting, not just a simple hematoma.

Clinically, the patient has acute onset pain, proptosis, chemosis, decreased vision, and limited extraocular movements following trauma — a classic picture of orbital compartment syndrome, usually from retrobulbar hemorrhage.

Among the options, this combination of trauma, retrobulbar hematoma, proptosis, and imaging evidence of globe tenting is most consistent with:

Answer: E

title: Case number 18775
raw:
Imaging shows a relatively homogeneous, poorly enhancing mass at the pancreatic head, causing obstructive jaundice and a long‑segment smooth stricture of the common bile duct with upstream intra‑ and extrahepatic biliary dilatation. On follow‑up (“post‑treatment”) MRI/CT, both the pancreatic head enlargement and the biliary narrowing markedly regress.

This pattern of a pancreatic head mass with associated bile duct involvement that dramatically improves after medical therapy is classic for type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis with IgG4‑related sclerosing cholangitis. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, lymphoma, plasmacytoma, or metastases would not show such rapid, near-complete resolution after short‑term treatment and typically produce different ductal and enhancement patterns.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18785
raw:
The images show a well‑circumscribed solid pancreatic lesion with strong uptake on 18F‑choline PET and marked arterial hyperenhancement on MRI, with washout on later phases and restricted diffusion. There is no obvious pancreatic duct obstruction or infiltrative, hypovascular pattern to suggest conventional ductal adenocarcinoma. In an elderly man, an incidentally discovered, hypervascular pancreatic mass with these MRI features is most consistent with a pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasm rather than acinar cell carcinoma, solid pseudopapillary tumor, or pancreatoblastoma (which are either less hypervascular or occur in much younger patients).  

Answer: C

title: Case number 18788
raw:
The CT images show a small, well-circumscribed, round soft‑tissue nodule with relatively homogeneous attenuation (~60–70 HU) lying freely in the dependent pelvis, separate from bowel and mesentery. There is no associated mesenteric thickening, fat stranding, or attachment to the omentum.

- Omental infarction (A) would appear as a larger, fat-density, ill-defined omental lesion with surrounding inflammatory fat stranding, which is not present.
- Calcified mesenteric lymph node (B) would be fixed within the mesentery and usually have coarse calcification, not a free intraperitoneal round body.
- Foreign body (D) typically has a characteristic shape or very high attenuation and a clear history of introduction; this lesion is smooth and spherical.
- Gallstones in the peritoneal cavity (E) are usually calcified/highly attenuating and often located near the gallbladder fossa or prior surgical site; here the lesion is soft-tissue density and in the dependent pelvis.

A small, mobile, spherical soft-tissue nodule in the dependent peritoneum is characteristic of a loose peritoneal body (peritoneal mouse).

Answer: C

title: Case number 18789
raw:
CT abdomen shows symmetric perirenal soft-tissue “rind” (“hairy kidney”) and retroperitoneal soft-tissue encasing the great vessels (“coated aorta”). PET-CT demonstrates intense FDG uptake in these regions. CT chest reveals a right atrial/pericardial soft-tissue mass (“right atrial pseudotumor”), and brain MRI shows bilateral intraconal orbital soft tissue causing proptosis.

This combination of perirenal rind, coated aorta, cardiac pseudotumor, and bilateral orbital involvement is classic for Erdheim–Chester disease, a multisystem non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and is far more specific than patterns seen in IgG4-related disease, Rosai–Dorfman disease, lymphoma, or metastases.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18796
raw:
The imaging shows:

- Chest radiograph: bilateral diffuse opacities compatible with inhalation injury/ARDS.
- Abdominal CT: bilateral renal cortical hypoenhancement and areas of necrosis (circled), consistent with acute tubular necrosis/cortical necrosis.
- Brain CT: diffuse cerebral edema without focal stroke or hemorrhage.

In the context of a workplace accident with molten chemicals causing extensive third-degree burns, immediate unconsciousness (GCS 3), severe inhalation injury, hypotension, and rapidly developing oligo-anuria with radiologic evidence of renal cortical necrosis and multiorgan injury, this pattern is characteristic of systemic toxicity from dermal/inhalational absorption of phenol (carbolic acid), a caustic chemical well known to cause severe burns plus direct renal and CNS toxicity.

The findings are not consistent with septic shock (which would usually be later and associated with clear infectious foci), nor with stroke or myocardial infarction, and the scenario is specific for phenol rather than an unspecified other caustic agent.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18797
raw:
The splenic lesion is a solitary, well-circumscribed mass in an otherwise normal spleen of an asymptomatic 66‑year‑old woman.  

Imaging:
- CT and MRI show a heterogeneous lesion with a central stellate low-attenuation/low-signal scar and radiating septa.
- The mass is predominantly T2 hypointense relative to the spleen and enhances in a progressive, nodular/“spoke-wheel” pattern rather than behaving like a classic haemangioma (which would be T2 markedly hyperintense with cavernous fill-in) or lymphoma (which is usually multiple, homogeneous, and without a central scar).

Pathology:
- Grossly, the cut surface shows a multinodular, tan lesion with fibrous areas.
- Histology demonstrates multiple angiomatoid nodules separated by dense fibrosclerotic stroma and rich inflammatory infiltrate rather than sheets of atypical lymphoid cells (lymphoma), spindle myofibroblasts (IMT), or a follicular dendritic cell neoplasm (EBV-positive FDCS).

This constellation is characteristic of sclerosing angiomatoid nodular transformation of the spleen.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18802
raw:
The radiographs show numerous calcified loose bodies in the suprapatellar pouch and along the joint line. MRI demonstrates a large joint effusion with countless intra‑articular nodules that are high signal on T2 and intermediate on T1, some with low‑signal rims corresponding to mineralization. The distribution is intra-articular and monoarticular in the knee, with no features of diffuse fatty villous synovium (lipoma arborescens), hemosiderin-laden synovium (TGCT/PVNS), vascular channels (synovial hemangioma), or erosive polyarthritis (RA).

These findings are classic for primary synovial chondromatosis.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18803
raw:
The images show a very large, well-circumscribed, predominantly homogeneous soft-tissue mass arising from the right pleural surface, forming obtuse angles with the chest wall and compressing the adjacent lung without diffuse pleural thickening or significant effusion. PET-CT demonstrates intense FDG uptake within this solitary pleural-based lesion.

This morphology—a single, often massive, extrapulmonary, pleural-based mass with smooth margins and lung compression—is classic for a solitary fibrous tumour of the pleura.  

Malignant mesothelioma typically presents with diffuse pleural thickening and effusion rather than a single large encapsulated mass. Teratoma and thymoma are usually mediastinal and often contain fat or calcification (teratoma) or are not pleural-based (thymoma). Pleural schwannoma is much rarer and typically smaller and associated with an intercostal nerve rather than such a huge pleural-based mass.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18808
raw:
The MRI shows a well-defined, predominantly cystic, multiloculated lesion in the presacral/retrorectal space, posterior to the rectum and anterior to the sacrum. It has high T2 signal, low T1 signal and no obvious solid enhancing component, consistent with a benign congenital cystic lesion. This location and appearance are classic for a tailgut cyst, which is a developmental cyst arising from remnants of the embryonic hindgut, most commonly seen incidentally in women during pelvic imaging.

Neurogenic tumours and neurofibromas are typically solid and often show characteristic enhancement patterns rather than a purely cystic, multilocular structure. Mesenchymal tumours are also usually solid. Incomplete Currarino syndrome requires associated sacral anomalies and anorectal malformations, which are not clearly present here; moreover, the primary lesion itself is most consistent with a tailgut cyst.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18809
raw:
MRI (DWI/ADC/FLAIR) shows acute small cortical/subcortical infarcts in the left hemisphere, matching the patient’s right-sided symptoms.

CTA neck (axial, coronal, sagittal) at the level of the internal carotid artery demonstrates a well-defined intraluminal filling defect surrounded by contrast, elongated along the artery and not causing complete occlusion. It appears pedunculated/off the wall rather than crescentic mural thickening or an ulcer cavity.

This is characteristic of a non-occlusive, intraluminal, mobile thrombus within the ICA—i.e., a free‑floating thrombus—serving as an embolic source for the acute infarcts.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18811
raw:
The imaging shows a localized, subcapsular cluster of numerous small cysts in the left hepatic lobe, with a “grape-like” appearance and no diffuse involvement of the liver or kidneys, arguing against autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease and Caroli disease. There is no obvious dominant papillary mass or marked upstream biliary dilatation to suggest intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile duct.  

On MRI/MRCP the lesion appears as a well‑demarcated multicystic mass rather than a single large macrocystic tumor typical of mucinous cystic neoplasm. Histology demonstrates multiple irregular cystically dilated bile duct structures lined by bland biliary-type epithelium within fibrous stroma, without ovarian-type stroma or significant papillary architecture, which is characteristic of multicystic biliary hamartoma.  

Taken together, the findings are most consistent with a multicystic biliary hamartoma of the liver.  

Answer: D

title: Case number 18813
raw:
The CT images show a homogeneous soft‑tissue mass diffusely infiltrating the right ventricular free wall and possibly extending into the right atrium, associated with a moderate pericardial effusion (yellow arrows). There is no classic bulky, exophytic intracavitary mass with hemorrhage/necrosis as seen in angiosarcoma or undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma.  

The PET/CT demonstrates intense FDG uptake centered in the heart, matching this infiltrative myocardial lesion, and a small focus in the lung likely secondary involvement. Echocardiography reported right‑ventricular thickening, and clinically the patient has a complete heart block and elevated troponins, consistent with myocardial and conduction system infiltration rather than a purely pericardial process.  

Primary cardiac lymphoma characteristically presents as a homogeneously enhancing, infiltrative mass involving the right heart (RA/RV), often with pericardial effusion, conduction abnormalities, and very high FDG uptake. Erdheim–Chester disease and IgG4‑related disease would typically show characteristic systemic manifestations (periaortic, perirenal, osseous, etc.) that are not evident here.  

Thus, the constellation of an infiltrative right‑sided cardiac mass, marked FDG avidity, pericardial effusion, and AV block best fits primary cardiac lymphoma.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18819
raw:
Extremely high AFP levels (>53,000 µg/L) in a testicular mass indicate a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor with strong yolk sac differentiation.  
Ultrasound shows a large heterogeneous, predominantly solid testicular mass with cystic/necrotic components and marked vascularity, without macroscopic fat or calcifications (which would suggest teratoma or mixed teratoma). Seminoma and lymphoma are not associated with such AFP elevation.  

These findings are most consistent with a pure yolk sac tumour.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18821
raw:
MR diffusion and FLAIR show acute cortical/subcortical infarcts in the right frontal lobe, explaining the left hemiparesis.  
CTA/DSA demonstrate severe narrowing/absence of the right ICA with a dense network of basal collateral vessels (“puff of smoke” appearance), consistent with moyamoya-type collaterals.  

The axial CT through the skull base shows a markedly small bony carotid canal on the affected side, indicating congenital ICA hypoplasia rather than acquired atherosclerotic, vasculitic, or dissecting disease. The contralateral ICA appears normal, arguing against primary bilateral moyamoya disease.

Thus, this represents a moyamoya pattern secondary to ICA hypoplasia.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18823
raw:
Mammography shows no suspicious mass, distortion, or calcifications in either breast, arguing against a primary breast carcinoma.  
Axillary ultrasound demonstrates multiple enlarged but oval lymph nodes with preserved fatty hila and benign-appearing vascularity, more typical of reactive/infectious lymphadenopathy than metastatic nodes.  

Histology of the biopsied node shows reactive follicular hyperplasia with clusters of epithelioid histiocytes and a mixed inflammatory background, without metastatic carcinoma or features of lymphoma. This pattern is characteristic of toxoplasmic lymphadenitis rather than granulomatous (e.g., TB/sarcoid) or lymphoproliferative disease.  

With isolated axillary lymphadenopathy, benign imaging of the breast, and histology compatible with toxoplasmic infection, the most likely diagnosis is toxoplasmic lymphadenopathy.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18824
raw:
The images show a lobulated, highly vascular mass arising from the gastric wall.  
CT demonstrates a strongly enhancing heterogeneous lesion in the stomach region with serpiginous vascular channels.  
Ultrasound and Doppler confirm a markedly vascular intramural mass.  
Histology reveals numerous dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces lined by endothelium in a lobular pattern, consistent with a cavernous-type vascular lesion rather than a spindle-cell (GIST) or gland-forming (carcinoma/metastasis) tumour.

These findings best fit a gastric haemangioma.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18829
raw:
The initial CT shows a well-circumscribed fat-attenuation mass in the right ischiorectal fossa. Five years later, CT and MRI demonstrate a markedly enlarged, heterogeneous mass extending from the ischiorectal fossa into the pelvis, with mixed fat and non-fat soft-tissue components. This evolution from a predominantly fatty lesion to a large, heterogeneous mass with solid elements is characteristic of a liposarcoma (often arising in or mimicking a pre-existing lipoma).

Dermoid cysts and extragonadal germ cell tumours typically show calcifications and other tissue types rather than this pattern, and tailgut cysts or anterior sacral meningoceles are fluid-filled, presacral, and not primarily fatty nor arising in the ischiorectal fossa.

Therefore, the best diagnosis is:

Answer: B

title: Case number 18838
raw:
The clinical photo shows a large, rounded mass directly over the acromioclavicular (AC) region.  
On the radiograph, there is a soft‑tissue mass superficial to the AC joint and marked superior migration of the humeral head, consistent with a chronic massive rotator cuff tear.  

Ultrasound demonstrates a mainly cystic lesion (*), communicating with the AC joint (Ac‑Cl label), and separate images show absence/marked thinning of the rotator cuff over the humeral head—again indicating a massive cuff tear.  

This combination of an AC‑region cystic mass with imaging evidence of a massive rotator cuff tear best fits an acromioclavicular cyst secondary to rotator cuff arthropathy rather than a primary soft‑tissue tumor or isolated degenerative AC changes.

Answer: E

title: Case number 18843
raw:
The imaging shows multiple large, expansile, homogeneous, low-attenuation lesions filling and remodeling the paranasal sinuses, with thinning and outward bowing of sinus walls and extension into the orbit causing ptosis/strabismus. The lesions are cystic, non-solid, and cause pressure remodeling rather than destructive bone lysis. MRI demonstrates uniform signal intensity with minimal enhancement, consistent with mucus-filled cavities rather than solid tumor.  

Histology shows respiratory mucosa with chronic inflammatory changes and mucus-filled spaces, without neoplastic epithelium or invasive organisms, which excludes malignancy, inverted papilloma, and actinomycosis. The size, expansile nature, and bony remodeling also go beyond a simple mucus retention cyst.  

These findings are classic for obstructive paranasal sinus mucoceles.  

Answer: E

title: Case number 18851
raw:
The CT shows multiple, small, intensely enhancing subpleural nodules. On mediastinal and 3D reconstructions, these nodules are clearly connected by tortuous vessels to arteries along the chest wall (likely intercostal or internal mammary), with further communication to pulmonary vessels. The lesions are entirely vascular, with feeding branches arising from systemic arteries rather than from the pulmonary arterial tree, and there is no solid parenchymal component as would be expected for metastases.

This configuration best corresponds to an abnormal systemic-to-pulmonary vascular communication rather than a classic pulmonary AVM (pulmonary artery–to–pulmonary vein), pulmonary varix, or isolated pulmonary arterial aneurysm.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18855
raw:
Cardiac MRI cine images show mitral valve prolapse with mitral annular disjunction of the inferolateral wall. Late gadolinium enhancement demonstrates focal mid‑wall/inferolateral basal fibrosis just beneath the posterior mitral leaflet, not a coronary-territory subendocardial pattern. Coronary CT angiography (last image) shows no significant LCx disease, arguing against ischemic infarction. Basal septal thickness of 12 mm does not meet criteria for HCM.  

This pattern of focal inferolateral replacement fibrosis in the setting of MVP and ventricular arrhythmias is characteristic of mitral valve prolapse–related fibrosis.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18858
raw:
The imaging shows a subcutaneous, poorly marginated, heterogeneous mass in a 4‑month‑old infant’s arm. On MRI it is largely non‑fatty (intermediate signal on T1 compared to surrounding bright subcutaneous fat) with interspersed streaky components, and on ultrasound it has a heterogeneous echotexture with fibrous-appearing bands and limited vascularity.  

This pattern—triphasic mixture of fibrous tissue, fat, and primitive mesenchyme in a young infant, typically in the extremities—is characteristic of fibrous hamartoma of infancy rather than a predominantly fatty lesion such as lipoblastoma or lipoma, and it lacks the aggressive features expected with rhabdomyosarcoma or liposarcoma.

Answer: C

title: Case number 18859
raw:
The MR images show a markedly enlarged uterus with multiple leiomyomas. One dominant fibroid has central fluid-like signal with a thick enhancing rim and restricted diffusion on DWI/ADC, corresponding to a necrotic cavity filled with purulent material. The clinical context is a recently pregnant woman with fibroids who develops fever and persistent pelvic pain after a spontaneous abortion—typical for infection of a leiomyoma (pyomyoma). 

There is no imaging evidence of markedly abnormal endometrial contents (to suggest infected retained products), nor adnexal tubo‑ovarian collections (PID). Torsion or red degeneration of a fibroid usually causes infarction without the pronounced abscess-like central cavity and intense diffusion restriction seen here.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18861
raw:
CT (axial and coronal) shows a well‑circumscribed, round lesion in the gastric region with dense calcification, resembling a gallstone rather than soft‑tissue mass. It lies in/adjacent to the gastric wall, giving a submucosal bulge on endoscopy, with overlying mucosal ulceration. This appearance is not typical for adenocarcinoma or leiomyoma (which would be soft-tissue masses without such dense calcification) nor classic peptic ulcer disease.

These findings best fit a gallstone lodged in the gastric wall mimicking a submucosal tumor.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18877
raw:
The CT images show multiple post-tuberculous cavitary lesions in the upper lobes. Within one of these cavities, there is a contrast-filled saccular outpouching that is contiguous with a branch of the pulmonary artery, best seen on the axial and 3D reconstructed angiographic images. This represents a pseudoaneurysm of a peripheral pulmonary artery arising in the wall of a tuberculous cavity.

In a patient with prior pulmonary tuberculosis and acute massive haemoptysis, this appearance is classic for a Rasmussen aneurysm rather than an aspergilloma (would appear as a non-enhancing intracavitary mass) or a systemic/mycotic aneurysm, Behçet’s disease, or neoplasm.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18885
raw:
The images show a low-attenuation, cystic lesion arising from the wall of the popliteal artery, causing eccentric narrowing/occlusion of the arterial lumen. Duplex US demonstrates a cystic mass adjacent to the artery with preserved but narrowed flow. CT confirms a cystic structure within the arterial wall rather than an external mass (as would be seen with a Baker’s cyst). Operative images and specimen show a cyst in the adventitia of the artery.

This pattern is characteristic of cystic adventitial disease of the popliteal artery, which typically presents with claudication and absent distal pulses in otherwise healthy middle-aged patients.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18886
raw:
The MRI demonstrates a split spinal cord at the thoracic level with two hemicords separated by a midline low-signal septum, consistent with an osseous/fibrous spur (as indicated by the dashed arrow on the axial image). This corresponds to a type I split cord malformation, classically termed diastematomyelia, rather than a simple syrinx or an intradural cyst.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18889
raw:
The CT images show a duplicated left collecting system with two ureters. One ureter follows the normal course to the bladder, while the other, highlighted by the arrowheads, runs medially and descends past the bladder to terminate ectopically in the pelvic floor region (likely the vagina/urethra). This explains the patient’s recurrent infections and hematuria and matches a duplex collecting system with an ectopic ureter, rather than a bladder diverticulum, ureterocele, hemirenal fusion, or vesicovaginal fistula.

Answer: D

title: Case number 18890
raw:
Orbital MRI shows bilateral choroidal detachments with thickened, enhancing posterior sclera—compatible with posterior scleritis and choroidal effusions. Chest CT demonstrates bilateral hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy with upper-lobe nodules, and the patient has elevated serum ACE. This combination of ocular inflammation plus typical thoracic findings and raised ACE is characteristic of sarcoidosis, which can present with posterior scleritis and choroidal detachments.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18898
raw:
The CT images show a very large, lobulated, predominantly soft-tissue mass arising from the anterior thoracic wall, contiguous with the costal arches, with internal arc-like calcifications and cortical destruction, extending both outward (into the breast region) and inward, compressing the lung and heart. This exophytic, cartilage-matrix, bone-destroying tumor of a rib/costal cartilage is characteristic of a chest wall chondrosarcoma rather than a benign enchondroma (which would be smaller, intramedullary, and less aggressive) or a neurogenic tumor (usually posterior, without chondroid calcification). Synovial sarcoma or metastasis would not typically demonstrate this pattern of chondroid calcification and rib-origin.

Answer: A

title: Case number 18899
raw:
The midline suprapubic mass in this 3‑month-old girl is cystic on ultrasound, arising from the pelvis and extending into the abdomen, lying posterior to the pubic symphysis and separate from the urinary bladder. The perineal image shows drainage through the vaginal/hymenal area rather than from the urethra. In this age group, a distended uterus and vagina filled with noninfected secretions due to outflow obstruction (typically imperforate hymen or vaginal atresia) is classic for hydrometrocolpos. Hemato‑ and pyometrocolpos are unlikely in a 3‑month-old (no menses; no clear signs of pus), and the appearance/location do not fit an ovarian mass or simple bladder distension.

Answer: B

title: Case number 18903
raw:
The imaging shows a huge expansile, multilobulated, predominantly lytic lesion around the proximal femur/acetabular region with some internal calcified foci and associated soft‑tissue mass. PET demonstrates intense metabolic activity.

Histology (H&E) reveals amorphous eosinophilic extracellular deposits with minimal cellularity. The Congo red stain under polarized light shows characteristic apple‑green birefringence, confirming amyloid deposition.

Clinically, the patient has markedly elevated IgG lambda paraprotein, indicating an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia, which commonly leads to AL (light‑chain) amyloidosis. The combination of paraproteinemia, destructive bone lesion, and histologic confirmation of amyloid firmly supports bone amyloidosis.

Other choices:
- Aneurysmal bone cyst – would show blood-filled cystic spaces; not compatible with Congo red–positive amyloid.
- Post‑traumatic granulation tissue – would not produce such massive lytic destruction or Congo red–positive deposits.
- Myeloma – explains paraproteinemia but histology here is amyloid, not sheets of plasma cells.
- Fibrous dysplasia – shows “ground glass” matrix, not amorphous amyloid deposits.

Thus the most likely diagnosis is bone amyloidosis.

title: Case number 18919

title: Case number 18927

title: Case number 18969

title: Case number 18974

title: Case number 19011

title: Case number 19030

- Hypoxic-ischemic and nonspecific toxic-metabolic encephalopathy would not preferentially involve the corpus callosum in this way.

title: Case number 19031

title: Case number 19067

title: Case number 19070

title: Case number 19078

title: Case number 19099

The initial radiographs (2014) show a well‑defined, geographic, lytic lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis with a narrow zone of transition and thin cortical shell, so it was appropriately considered benign at that time.

By 2022, CT and MRI demonstrate a markedly enlarged, expansile lesion with:

- Thick, nodular solid components and septa that avidly enhance.

title: Case number 19109

title: Case number 19115

title: Case number 19116

The imaging pattern and patient demographics best match an ovarian dysgerminoma.

title: Case number 19137

title: Case number 19161

title: Case number 19172

title: Case number 19221
